extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of periodical social essays (early-18th-century general readership); essayists interested in character sketching and social observation
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and practical observations for composing short periodical essays and character sketches that report on social life, theatre, and manners; includes authorial attitudes toward fame and audience-tailoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre architecture must preserve actors' audibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A house that is too large, and its architecture, can 'swallow up the voices of the actors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Vanbrugh's Haymarket initially failed partly because the building was too large and the architecture swallowed actors' voices; practical remedy used later: 'contracted the width of the theatre, brought down its enormously high ceiling, thus made the words of the plays audible.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialize theatre programming (separate opera and plays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatres can succeed by specialising: one house devoted to plays, another to opera, with coordinated scheduling and licensing arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical arrangement described: agreement that 'Drury Lane' would confine itself to acting plays while the 'Haymarket' devoted itself to opera; included scheduling (closing Drury Lane on Wednesdays when an opera was played) and financial terms (actors paying for use of a license).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character eccentricities should stem from intelligible motives
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's oddities (singularities) should proceed from good sense or clear motives rather than sourness or obstinacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Sir Roger de Coverley: his singularities are 'Contradictions to the Manners of the World, only as he thinks the World is in the wrong.' This produces a pleasing, non-hostile eccentricity: he 'does nothing with Sourness or Obstinacy' and so creates no enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray characters through concrete social roles and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Define characters by their social station, habitual practices, and the effect they have on others (tenants, servants, visitors), using concrete details and anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sir Roger's household, his being a Justice of the Quorum, his coat and doublet remaining from a past fashion, tenants growing rich and servants satisfied; Will Honeycomb's knowledge of fashions and female world documented via specific conversational examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial aim: write to satisfy your own mind, not to chase fame
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should care primarily to satisfy his own mind and design, and be 'negligent of the Consequences' (fame, reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advised practice: avoid anxious pursuit of reputation; be 'very careful of the Design of my Actions, but very negligent of the Consequences of them.' Anecdote: obsessing over fame is 'endless and frivolous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use silence and solitary observation as tools for insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Resignation of speech and a habit of silence grant heightened powers of observation and penetration into people's characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator claims that being silent in public yields advantages: he sees men 'with an unprejudiced Eye', makes shrewd guesses about their thoughts without being admitted to their conversation, and derives material for writing from the sights and gestures he observes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor style and tone to the intended audience (e.g., women)
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing a particular audience (here, women), adapt style, air, and topics to suit their understanding and interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit promise: 'When it is a Woman's Day, in my Works, I shall endeavour at a Stile and Air suitable to their Understanding.' The author plans to 'lead the young through all the becoming Duties of Virginity, Marriage, and Widowhood,' dedicating a share of speculations to their service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer honest, measured praise over flattery or falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain honesty in commentary: do not flatter falsely, but also avoid lying or contradiction in critique of others, particularly of women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial stance: 'If I never praised or flattered, I never belyed or contradicted them.' This indicates a principle of temperate, sincere description rather than exaggeration or defamation.
